claims.text: The initial arc-melted, cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy is nominally a single-phase disordered BCC material.
Annealing followed by slow cooling promotes local chemical short-range order or atomic clustering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Rapid quenching retains a maximally disordered HfNbTaTiZr configuration.
HfNbTaTiZr has significant atomic mobility over 500–1200 °C.
The range 500–1200 °C is well below melting and large-scale phase-transformation limits for the tested material.
Temperature-induced local chemical short-range order modifies local bonding environments in HfNbTaTiZr.
Annealing causes preferential clustering of particular element pairs, proposed examples being Ta–Nb and Hf–Zr.
Preferential elemental clustering alters local bond stiffness.
Preferential elemental clustering enhances anharmonic lattice vibrations.
Changes in bond anharmonicity govern elevated-temperature stress–strain, thermal-expansion, and elastic responses.
Short-range-order-driven bond rearrangement reduces the effective thermal expansion.
Short-range-order-driven bond rearrangement modifies elastic modulus and yield behavior by changing lattice stability against deformation.
Relative to quenched samples, slowly cooled samples with enhanced short-range order will have a systematically lower thermal-expansion coefficient.
Relative to quenched samples, slowly cooled samples will likely retain a slightly higher elastic modulus at elevated temperatures.
Relative to quenched samples, slowly cooled samples will show a shifted yield point.
A shifted yield point would indicate altered dislocation activity or lattice resistance.
Below the proposed temperature range, insufficient atomic mobility may prevent the hypothesized ordering effect.
Above the proposed temperature range, other phase transformations may confound the hypothesized mechanism.
